title: Building the Transformer Block
description: Assemble the complete Transformer block: positional encoding to restore order, residual connections and layer normalization for stable deep training, the feed-forward sublayer, and how it all fits together.

lessons.title: Positional Encoding
lessons.description: Learn how Transformers inject word order back into a mechanism that otherwise has no built-in sense of position.

sections.title: What you should be able to do
sections.content: By the end of this lesson, you can explain why Transformers need positional encoding and how it's typically added to the input.

sections.title: 🤷 The problem: self-attention has no sense of order
sections.content: Look back at the scaled dot-product attention formula: it computes relevance based purely on the *content* of queries and keys — nothing about it inherently knows which word came first, second, or last in the sequence. Unlike an RNN, which processes words strictly in order, self-attention treats the sequence more like an unordered set — mathematically, shuffling the input words would produce the exact same set of pairwise relevance computations. But word order clearly matters for meaning (recall the NLP course's "dog bit man" vs. "man bit dog" example) — so this information needs to be added back in some way.

sections.title: 📍 The fix: adding a position signal to each embedding
sections.content:
**Positional encoding** adds information about each token's position directly into its embedding, before self-attention is applied — giving the model a way to distinguish "word in position 1" from "the same word in position 5."

```python
# Conceptual
# final_input = token_embedding + positional_encoding
```

The original Transformer paper used a fixed mathematical formula based on sine and cosine waves at different frequencies, generating a unique pattern of values for each position — chosen partly because it lets the model potentially generalize to sequence lengths not seen during training.

sections.title: 🎓 A learned alternative
sections.content: An alternative approach, used by some models (including early versions of BERT and GPT), simply **learns** a separate embedding vector for each position, exactly like a word gets a learned embedding, treating "position 5" as its own thing to be learned rather than computed by a fixed formula. This is simpler to implement, though it typically can't generalize as well beyond sequence lengths seen during training, since a specific position number that never appeared in training has no learned embedding at all.

sections.title: Common mistakes
sections.content:
**Assuming self-attention has some inherent sense of word order.** It genuinely doesn't — positional encoding is a necessary, deliberate addition, not an optional nice-to-have.

**Confusing positional encoding with the token embeddings themselves.** They're typically combined (often simply added together) to produce the actual input to the Transformer — position and content are represented together, but they come from two conceptually distinct sources.

**Assuming there's only one "correct" way to encode position.** As later lessons in this course cover, several different approaches (fixed sinusoidal, learned, and more modern alternatives like RoPE) have been developed, each with different tradeoffs.

questions.question: Why does self-attention need positional encoding, unlike an RNN?
options: Self-attention cannot process more than one word without positional encoding
Self-attention computes relevance based purely on content, with no inherent sense of word order — unlike an RNN, which processes words sequentially and naturally has order built in
RNNs also require positional encoding, so there's no real difference
Positional encoding is only needed for very short sequences
questions.explanation: Since self-attention's relevance computation depends only on the content of queries and keys, shuffling the input words would produce the same pairwise relevance scores — order has to be explicitly reintroduced, unlike an RNN which processes tokens in sequence by design.

questions.question: How is positional encoding typically combined with token embeddings?
options: It replaces the token embedding entirely
It's typically added directly to the token embedding, so the final input represents both content and position together
It's stored completely separately and never actually used by the model
Positional encoding is applied only after the entire Transformer has finished processing
questions.explanation: Positional encoding is generated per position and added to the corresponding token's embedding, so the resulting combined vector carries information about both what the token is and where it appears in the sequence.

questions.question: What is a potential drawback of using learned positional embeddings instead of a fixed sinusoidal formula?
options: Learned embeddings are always less accurate
Learned embeddings typically can't generalize as well to sequence lengths not seen during training, since an unseen position has no learned embedding at all
Learned embeddings cannot be used with self-attention
There is no real tradeoff between the two approaches
questions.explanation: Since learned positional embeddings are trained specifically for positions seen during training, a position number that never appeared (like a much longer sequence than any training example) has no meaningful learned embedding — a fixed formula-based approach can extend more naturally to new lengths.

questions.question: Why does self-attention, unlike an RNN, need an explicit mechanism to represent word order?
options: Self-attention cannot process sequences of more than one word
Self-attention computes relevance based purely on content, so shuffling the input would produce the same pairwise relevance computations
RNNs also lack any sense of word order
Word order does not matter for meaning in any language
questions.explanation: Self-attention's relevance computation depends only on the content of queries and keys, so without an explicit positional signal, shuffling the input words would produce identical pairwise relevance scores — order must be added back in.

questions.question: What mathematical functions did the original Transformer paper use to compute fixed positional encodings?
options: Logarithms and exponentials
Sine and cosine waves at different frequencies
Random number generation with no formula
Simple integer counting from 1 to the sequence length
questions.explanation: The original Transformer paper used a fixed formula based on sine and cosine waves at different frequencies to generate a unique positional pattern for each position.

questions.question: What is a key potential benefit of the fixed sinusoidal positional encoding approach mentioned in this lesson?
options: It requires no computation at all
It may let the model generalize to sequence lengths not seen during training
It always outperforms every learned alternative on every task
It removes the need for token embeddings entirely
questions.explanation: The fixed sinusoidal formula was chosen partly because it can potentially let the model generalize to sequence lengths beyond what it saw during training, unlike some learned alternatives.

questions.question: How do learned positional embeddings, used by some models like early BERT and GPT versions, work?
options: They use the exact same sine/cosine formula as the original Transformer
A separate embedding vector is learned for each position, exactly like a word gets a learned embedding
They require no training of any kind
Positional information is entirely omitted from the model
questions.explanation: Learned positional embeddings simply learn a separate embedding vector for each position during training, treating each position number as its own thing to learn, similar to how word embeddings are learned.

questions.question: What is a drawback of learned positional embeddings compared to the fixed sinusoidal approach?
options: Learned embeddings are always more computationally expensive
They typically can't generalize as well to sequence lengths not seen during training, since an unseen position has no learned embedding
Learned embeddings cannot be combined with token embeddings at all
There is no meaningful drawback whatsoever
questions.explanation: Since learned positional embeddings are trained only for the specific positions seen during training, a position number never encountered in training (like an unusually long sequence) has no meaningful learned representation.

lessons.title: Residual Connections and Layer Normalization
lessons.description: Learn the two supporting techniques that make it practical to stack many Transformer layers deep.

sections.title: What you should be able to do
sections.content: By the end of this lesson, you can explain why residual connections and layer normalization are used throughout the Transformer architecture.

sections.title: 🔁 Residual connections: a familiar idea from computer vision
sections.content:
Recall ResNet's skip connections from the computer vision course: shortcuts that let information (and gradients) bypass layers directly, helping very deep networks train effectively. Transformers use the exact same idea throughout: each sublayer's output is added to its own input, rather than completely replacing it.

```
# Conceptual residual connection around a sublayer
output = sublayer(input) + input
```

Just as in ResNet, this gives gradients a more direct path back through many stacked layers during backpropagation, which is essential for training the many-layers-deep Transformer stacks used in practice.

sections.title: 📏 Layer normalization: keeping values well-behaved
sections.content:
Recall batch normalization from the deep learning course, which normalizes activations using statistics computed across a mini-batch. **Layer normalization** is a related but distinct technique — instead of normalizing across the batch, it normalizes across the *features* of a single example, independent of batch size or other examples.

This distinction matters practically: layer normalization doesn't depend on batch statistics, making it well-suited to sequence models where batch composition and sequence length can vary, and it's the standard normalization choice throughout Transformer architectures.

sections.title: 🏗️ How they combine in a Transformer sublayer
sections.content:
```
# Conceptual structure of one Transformer sublayer
output = LayerNorm(input + Sublayer(input))
# where Sublayer is either self-attention or the feed-forward layer (next lesson)
```

This specific combination — residual connection plus layer normalization, wrapped around each individual sublayer — is applied consistently throughout the entire Transformer architecture, and is a major reason very deep Transformer stacks (many layers) can be trained effectively and stably.

sections.title: Common mistakes
sections.content:
**Confusing layer normalization with batch normalization.** They solve a related problem (keeping activations well-scaled) but normalize across different dimensions (features of one example vs. a mini-batch) — this distinction is exactly why layer norm suits sequence models better.

**Underestimating how essential residual connections are for Transformer depth.** Without them, training the many-layer-deep stacks used in real Transformer models would face serious difficulties, directly echoing the vanishing gradient problem from the deep learning course.

**Treating this as a minor implementation detail.** These two techniques, applied consistently throughout the architecture, are a significant part of what makes training very deep Transformer models practical and stable at all.

questions.question: What do residual connections in a Transformer do, echoing an idea from the computer vision course?
options: They remove the need for any self-attention layers
They add a sublayer's output to its own input, providing a shortcut that helps gradients flow through many stacked layers during training, just like ResNet's skip connections
They convert text tokens directly into images
They eliminate the need for positional encoding
questions.explanation: Just as ResNet's skip connections let information bypass layers directly to help train very deep CNNs, Transformer residual connections add each sublayer's output back to its input, giving gradients a more direct path through many stacked Transformer layers.

questions.question: How does layer normalization differ from the batch normalization covered in the deep learning course?
options: They are identical techniques with different names
Layer normalization normalizes across the features of a single example, independent of batch composition, while batch normalization normalizes using statistics computed across a mini-batch
Layer normalization can only be used with images, not text
Batch normalization is never actually used in deep learning
questions.explanation: The key difference is what's being normalized across — layer norm operates per-example across its own features, making it independent of batch size or composition, which is why it suits sequence models (with variable batch/sequence characteristics) better than batch norm.

questions.question: Why are residual connections considered essential for training very deep Transformer stacks?
options: They have no real effect on training and are purely a stylistic choice
Without them, training many stacked layers would face serious difficulties, echoing the vanishing gradient problem from the deep learning course that ResNet's skip connections were designed to solve
They only matter for very short sequences
Residual connections replace the need for self-attention entirely
questions.explanation: The same core problem that motivated ResNet's skip connections in computer vision — difficulty training very deep stacks due to gradient issues — applies to deep Transformer stacks as well, which is why residual connections are used consistently throughout the architecture.

questions.question: What earlier architecture from the computer vision course does this lesson compare residual connections to?
options: Vision Transformers
ResNet's skip connections
AlexNet's pooling layers
YOLO's detection heads
questions.explanation: This lesson draws a direct comparison to ResNet's skip connections from the computer vision course, which let information bypass layers directly to help train very deep networks.

questions.question: In the conceptual formula for a residual connection given in this lesson, what is added to a sublayer's output?
options: The sublayer's output is left completely unchanged, with nothing added
The sublayer's own input
A randomly generated noise vector
The output of a completely different, unrelated sublayer
questions.explanation: The residual connection formula is output = sublayer(input) + input — the sublayer's output is added back to its own input rather than replacing it entirely.

questions.question: What does layer normalization normalize across, in contrast to batch normalization?
options: Layer norm normalizes across a mini-batch, exactly like batch norm
Layer norm normalizes across the features of a single example, independent of batch composition
Layer norm and batch norm normalize across identical dimensions
Layer norm normalizes across an entire dataset at once
questions.explanation: Layer normalization normalizes across the features of a single example rather than across a mini-batch, making it independent of batch size or composition — unlike batch normalization from the deep learning course.

questions.question: Why does layer normalization suit sequence models particularly well, according to this lesson?
options: It requires a fixed, unchanging batch size at all times
It doesn't depend on batch statistics, making it well suited to sequence models where batch composition and sequence length can vary
It can only be applied to image data
It eliminates the need for any residual connections
questions.explanation: Since layer normalization doesn't rely on statistics computed across a batch, it handles the variable batch composition and sequence lengths common in sequence models more naturally than batch normalization.

questions.question: What is the conceptual formula given in this lesson for combining a residual connection with layer normalization around a sublayer?
options: Sublayer(LayerNorm(input))
LayerNorm(input + Sublayer(input))
input - Sublayer(LayerNorm(input))
LayerNorm(input) alone, with no residual connection
questions.explanation: The lesson gives LayerNorm(input + Sublayer(input)) as the standard structure — the residual connection is added first, then layer normalization is applied to the result.

lessons.title: The Feed-Forward Sublayer
lessons.description: Learn about the other essential piece of a Transformer block, working alongside self-attention.

sections.title: What you should be able to do
sections.content: By the end of this lesson, you can describe the feed-forward sublayer's role within a Transformer block.

sections.title: 🧩 A Transformer block has two main sublayers
sections.content: Each Transformer block (or "layer") consists of two main sublayers, each wrapped in the residual-connection-plus-layer-norm pattern from the previous lesson: the **self-attention sublayer** (module 0) and a **feed-forward sublayer** — a comparatively simple, fully-connected network.

sections.title: 🔢 What the feed-forward sublayer actually does
sections.content:
The feed-forward sublayer is a small, standard fully-connected network (recall these from the deep learning course) applied **independently and identically to each position** in the sequence — unlike self-attention, it doesn't mix information *between* different positions at all; it just transforms each position's representation on its own, using the exact same learned weights at every position.

```python
# Conceptual: applied independently at every position
# def feed_forward(x):
#     return linear2(relu(linear1(x)))
# — the same linear1, linear2 weights are reused at every sequence position
```

Typically, the hidden layer inside this feed-forward network is considerably wider than the token embedding dimension itself, giving the block extra capacity to transform each position's representation.

sections.title: 🤝 Why both pieces are needed together
sections.content: Self-attention handles mixing information *between* positions — figuring out which other words are relevant to this one. The feed-forward sublayer then processes *each* position's resulting representation further, independently. Together, a Transformer block alternates between these two very different kinds of operations: mix across positions (attention), then transform each position independently (feed-forward) — repeated across many stacked layers, gradually building increasingly rich, sophisticated representations.

sections.title: Common mistakes
sections.content:
**Assuming the feed-forward sublayer mixes information across positions, like self-attention does.** It explicitly does not — it's applied identically and independently to each position, with no interaction between different positions within this particular sublayer.

**Underestimating the feed-forward sublayer's contribution.** Despite conceptually being the "simpler" of the two sublayers, it typically contains a substantial share of a Transformer model's total learnable parameters, given its wider hidden layer.

**Forgetting the residual connection and layer norm wrap around this sublayer too.** Exactly the same pattern from the previous lesson (`LayerNorm(input + Sublayer(input))`) applies to the feed-forward sublayer, just as it does to self-attention.

questions.question: How is the feed-forward sublayer applied across a sequence, in contrast to self-attention?
options: It mixes information across all positions simultaneously, exactly like self-attention
It's applied independently and identically to each position, using the same learned weights, without mixing information between different positions
It only processes the very first token in the sequence
It requires a completely separate set of weights for every single position
questions.explanation: Unlike self-attention, which explicitly relates different positions to each other, the feed-forward sublayer transforms each position's representation on its own, applying the exact same learned weights at every position independently.

questions.question: What are the two main sublayers within a single Transformer block?
options: Convolution and pooling
Self-attention and a feed-forward network
Encoding and decoding
Tokenization and embedding
questions.explanation: Each Transformer block combines a self-attention sublayer (which mixes information across positions) with a feed-forward sublayer (which independently transforms each position), both wrapped in residual connections and layer normalization.

questions.question: Why do self-attention and the feed-forward sublayer need to work together within a Transformer block?
options: They perform the exact same function and including both is redundant

Self-attention mixes information between positions, while the feed-forward sublayer further transforms each position's representation independently — together they build increasingly rich representations across stacked layers
Only the feed-forward sublayer actually contributes to the model's learning
Self-attention alone is always sufficient without any feed-forward component
questions.explanation: The two sublayers serve complementary roles: self-attention handles relating different positions to each other, while the feed-forward sublayer processes each position's resulting representation further — alternating between these across many layers builds up sophisticated representations.

questions.question: What are the two main sublayers that make up a single Transformer block, according to this lesson?
options: Convolution and pooling
Self-attention and a feed-forward sublayer
Encoder and decoder
Tokenization and embedding
questions.explanation: Each Transformer block consists of a self-attention sublayer and a feed-forward sublayer, each wrapped in the residual-connection-plus-layer-norm pattern from the previous lesson.

questions.question: How is the feed-forward sublayer applied across the positions in a sequence?
options: It mixes information across all positions, exactly like self-attention
It is applied independently and identically to each position, using the same learned weights at every position
It only processes the last position in the sequence
A completely separate set of weights is learned for every individual position
questions.explanation: Unlike self-attention, the feed-forward sublayer transforms each position's representation on its own, reusing the exact same learned weights (linear1, linear2) at every position independently.

questions.question: Compared to the token embedding dimension, how is the hidden layer inside the feed-forward sublayer typically sized?
options: It is always exactly the same size as the embedding dimension
It is typically considerably wider than the embedding dimension, giving the block extra transformation capacity
It is always smaller than the embedding dimension
The feed-forward sublayer has no hidden layer at all
questions.explanation: The feed-forward sublayer's hidden layer is typically considerably wider than the token embedding dimension, giving it extra capacity to transform each position's representation.

questions.question: What is a common misconception about the feed-forward sublayer's share of a Transformer model's total parameters?
options: That it always has zero learnable parameters
That it contributes only a negligible number of parameters, when in practice it often holds a substantial share, given its wider hidden layer
That it contains more parameters than every other component combined, always
That its parameter count is unrelated to its hidden layer width
questions.explanation: Despite being conceptually the 'simpler' sublayer, the feed-forward sublayer typically contains a substantial share of a Transformer model's total learnable parameters because of its wider hidden layer.

questions.question: Does the residual-connection-plus-layer-norm pattern from the previous lesson also apply to the feed-forward sublayer?
options: No, that pattern only applies to self-attention
Yes, the exact same LayerNorm(input + Sublayer(input)) pattern wraps the feed-forward sublayer too
The feed-forward sublayer uses a completely different, unrelated normalization scheme
Residual connections are only used once, at the very end of the whole model
questions.explanation: The same residual-connection-plus-layer-norm pattern established for self-attention also wraps the feed-forward sublayer, applying LayerNorm(input + Sublayer(input)) consistently to both sublayers.

lessons.title: Putting a Transformer Block Together
lessons.description: Assemble every piece from this module into the complete, standard Transformer block used throughout the architecture.

sections.title: What you should be able to do
sections.content: By the end of this lesson, you can describe the complete structure of a standard Transformer block, piece by piece.

sections.title: 🧱 The complete block, step by step
sections.content:
```
Input: token embeddings + positional encoding (previous lesson)

1. Multi-head self-attention (module 0)
2. Residual connection + layer normalization (this module)
3. Feed-forward sublayer (this module)
4. Residual connection + layer normalization (this module)

Output: a new representation for each position, ready for
        the next block (or the final output layer)
```

Every single piece covered in modules 0 and 1 comes together here into one repeatable, stackable unit.

sections.title: 📚 Stacking blocks to build a full model
sections.content:
A complete Transformer model stacks many of these identical blocks (structurally identical, though each has its own independently learned weights) on top of each other — the original Transformer paper used 6 encoder and 6 decoder blocks; modern large language models often stack dozens or more.

```python
# Conceptual: stacking N identical Transformer blocks
# x = token_embeddings + positional_encoding
# for _ in range(num_layers):
#     x = transformer_block(x)
# final_output = x
```

Each successive block can build on the increasingly rich, contextual representations produced by the blocks before it — similar in spirit to how a CNN's stacked layers (computer vision course) build from simple to complex features, though here it's through repeated attention and transformation, not spatial convolution.

sections.title: 🎯 Why this design has proven so effective
sections.content: This block design is genuinely elegant: it combines a mechanism for relating any two positions directly (self-attention), a mechanism for further per-position transformation (feed-forward), and the training stability tools (residuals, layer norm) needed to stack it very deep — all while being highly parallelizable across positions during training, unlike RNNs' inherently sequential processing. This combination of expressiveness, trainability, and parallelizability is a major reason the Transformer architecture became so dominant.

sections.title: Common mistakes
sections.content:
**Thinking of a Transformer block as a single, monolithic operation.** It's a specific, deliberate combination of several distinct pieces (attention, feed-forward, residuals, layer norm) — understanding each piece's individual role makes the whole design much clearer.

**Assuming every stacked block shares the same weights.** Each block has its own independently learned parameters — the *structure* is repeated identically, but the specific learned weights differ from block to block.

**Forgetting positional encoding is added once, at the very beginning.** It's not re-applied at every block — position information, once added to the initial input, propagates forward through the residual connections in every subsequent block.

questions.question: What is the correct order of operations within a standard Transformer block?
options: Feed-forward sublayer, then self-attention, with no normalization at all
Multi-head self-attention, then residual+layer norm, then the feed-forward sublayer, then another residual+layer norm
Positional encoding is recomputed at every single block
Layer normalization happens only once, at the very end of the entire model
questions.explanation: A standard Transformer block applies self-attention (wrapped in a residual connection and layer norm), followed by the feed-forward sublayer (also wrapped in its own residual connection and layer norm) — this exact repeatable structure is what gets stacked to build the full model.

questions.question: When a Transformer model stacks many blocks, do the blocks share the same learned weights?
options: Yes, every block uses identical weights throughout the model
No — each block has its own independently learned weights, even though the structural design is repeated identically across blocks
Only the first and last blocks have learned weights
Weights are shared, but only for the feed-forward sublayers
questions.explanation: While every block follows the same structural blueprint (self-attention, feed-forward, residuals, layer norm), each individual block learns its own separate set of weights during training — the repetition is in structure, not in the specific learned parameters.

questions.question: What combination of properties makes the Transformer block design particularly effective, according to this lesson?
options: It is the slowest possible architecture, which guarantees higher accuracy
It combines a mechanism for relating any two positions directly, per-position transformation, training stability techniques for depth, and high parallelizability during training
It requires no training data of any kind
It can only be used for very short sequences
questions.explanation: The Transformer block's effectiveness comes from combining several complementary strengths at once: self-attention's ability to directly relate any two positions, the feed-forward sublayer's per-position transformation, residual connections and layer norm enabling deep stacking, and strong parallelizability — unlike the sequential processing required by RNNs.

questions.question: According to this lesson, how many encoder and decoder blocks did the original Transformer paper use?
options: 1 encoder and 1 decoder block
6 encoder and 6 decoder blocks
100 encoder and 100 decoder blocks
The original paper used no decoder blocks at all
questions.explanation: The lesson notes that the original Transformer paper used 6 encoder and 6 decoder blocks, while modern large language models often stack dozens or more.

questions.question: When a Transformer model stacks many blocks together, do all the blocks share identical learned weights?
options: Yes, every block in the stack uses the exact same weights
No — each block has its own independently learned weights, even though the structural design repeats identically
Only the very first block has any learned weights
Weight sharing depends entirely on the specific input sequence
questions.explanation: While every stacked block follows the same structural blueprint, each individual block learns its own separate set of weights during training — repetition is in structure, not learned parameters.

questions.question: At what point in the overall model is positional encoding added, according to this lesson?
options: It is recomputed fresh at every single stacked block
It is added once, at the very beginning, and propagates forward through the residual connections in later blocks
It is added only at the very last block, right before the output
Positional encoding is never actually added to the input
questions.explanation: Positional encoding is added once to the initial input, and this positional information propagates forward through the residual connections in every subsequent stacked block, rather than being recomputed at each block.

questions.question: What combination of properties does this lesson credit for the Transformer block design's effectiveness?
options: Being the slowest possible design, which supposedly guarantees higher accuracy
Direct relationships between any two positions, per-position transformation, training-stability tools for depth, and strong parallelizability
Requiring no training data of any kind
Being usable only for extremely short sequences
questions.explanation: The lesson attributes the block design's effectiveness to combining self-attention's direct position-to-position relationships, per-position transformation via feed-forward, residuals/layer norm enabling deep stacking, and strong parallelizability — a combination hard to find together elsewhere.

questions.question: What analogy does this lesson draw between stacking Transformer blocks and a concept from the computer vision course?
options: It compares stacking blocks to convolutional filters detecting edges only
It compares each successive block building on richer representations to how a CNN's stacked layers build from simple to complex features
It claims there is no meaningful parallel to computer vision at all
It compares Transformer blocks to image resizing operations
questions.explanation: The lesson notes that each successive Transformer block can build on the increasingly rich representations from earlier blocks, similar in spirit to how a CNN's stacked layers build from simple to complex features, though through attention and transformation rather than convolution.
